title: Concatenation of Array
interviewTips: Clarify constraints: can you allocate a new array of size 2*n, or is in-place modification expected? For this problem output size differs, so extra space is required.

Trade-off to discuss: two explicit copy loops vs single loop with modulo vs language idioms like Python list concatenation — all are O(n) time and O(n) space, but single loop has fewer passes and cleaner index logic.
Edge-case tip: handle n=1, empty array if allowed, and confirm whether to mutate input or return new array; never assume nums length > 0 without check for modulo by zero.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force with Two Pass Copy
approaches.intuition: The definition directly says first half equals nums and second half equals nums. The most literal simulation is to create an array of size 2*n, copy nums into positions 0..n-1, then copy nums again into positions n..2*n-1.
approaches.theory: Allocate ans of length 2*n. First loop invariant: after iteration i, ans[0..i] holds nums[0..i]. Second loop invariant: after iteration i, ans[n..n+i] holds nums[0..i]. Together they establish ans[i]==nums[i] and ans[i+n]==nums[i] for all i. This uses two linear passes, each O(n), so total O(n) time and O(n) extra space for output.

timeComplexity.explanation: Two sequential loops each iterate n times where n = nums.length, so 2*n operations = O(n).

spaceComplexity.explanation: We allocate output array ans of size 2*n, which is required for the answer; auxiliary space beyond output is O(1).

edgeCases: n=1 e.g. nums=[1] => [1,1] — both loops run once
All equal values e.g. nums=[5,5,5] — verifies copy not aliasing
Max size n=1000 — 2*n allocation fits easily, no overflow

approaches.name: Approach 2: Optimal Single Pass with Modulo Indexing
approaches.intuition: Instead of thinking in two halves, think of ans as nums repeated periodically. Position i in ans should hold nums[i % n]. One loop over 2*n with modulo mapping fills both halves at once.
approaches.theory: For any i in [0, 2*n), i % n maps to [0, n). When i < n, i % n = i so ans[i]=nums[i]. When i >= n, i % n = i-n so ans[i]=nums[i-n], which is exactly ans[(i-n)+n]=nums[i-n]. This proves correctness in a single pass. It halves loop overhead and expresses the cyclic pattern generally usable for k-times repetition.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single loop over 2*n elements with O(1) modulo and assignment per iteration, so O(n) time.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Output array of size 2*n is required; only O(1) extra variables (n, i) are used.

edgeCases: Large values and negatives — modulo indexing unaffected by value range
Empty input if allowed: guard n==0 to avoid modulo by zero, return []
